A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across pagination and section changes.

before.justification: Figure 2 and Appendix H.1 report original transformer-training experiments and learned attention maps on first-, second-, and third-order Markov chains.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, and Appendices H.2–H.4 add original depth comparisons, noise robustness experiments, and quantization results.

M1.justification: Appendices B.1 and B.2 change the second MLP's coefficient multiplying v_n from 3/C_attn to 3 and update the reconstruction equation. This corrects a local scaling in the explicit construction; the overall architecture and two-stage training procedure are retained.

E1.justification: The original first- through third-order binary Markov coverage remains. Appendix H.3 adds second-order sequences with random token substitutions and time-varying transition perturbations, extending evaluation to two noisy input conditions within the same synthetic domain.

E2.justification: Appendix H.2 adds an experimentally evaluated one-layer transformer comparator against the two-layer model, with losses in Table 2 and attention maps in Figures 17–20. The cited architectures in Table 1 remain theoretical comparisons rather than newly evaluated empirical baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include a one-versus-two-layer comparison using shared hyperparameter ranges and excess cross-entropy, noise sweeps at levels 0, 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5, and weight-and-activation quantization at 2, 4, and 8 bits against a 32-bit reference. Appendix H.4 introduces numerical Frobenius attention-map error at sequence length 32. These substantially extend evaluation; the original general settings table is retained.

E4.justification: Appendices H.2–H.4 add complementary analyses of whether one-layer models learn induction patterns, how token corruption and transition perturbations affect performance, and how reduced precision affects attention alignment. v1 provides attention visualizations but lacks these depth, robustness, and precision studies.

E5.justification: v1 lists five repetitions without experimental mean-plus-standard-deviation summaries. v2 retains that general setting and adds explicitly labeled mean and standard deviation across three seeds for noise experiments and across ten different-kernel sequences for quantization. This establishes new uncertainty reporting, not increased repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports excess losses of 0.131 ± 0.000 for one layer and 0.100 ± 0.003 for two layers. Tables 3–4 report loss gaps reaching 0.21 under token noise and 0.181 under transition perturbations at level 0.5. Appendix H.4 adds Frobenius errors including 3.8615 at 8 bits and 3.7700 at 32 bits. These are new results, while the original attention-map findings are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects the reconstruction algebra. Table 1 and Remark 2 revise parameter-count formulas: for example, the proposed construction changes from 9d^2 + d(S + T) to 9d^2 + d(2T + 2S + 9), where d = 6S + 3. New Appendix I supplies component accounting. The main theorem statements, assumptions, and convergence results remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, boxed contributions, and conclusion retain the two-layer representation and first-order learnability claims. The introduction additionally asserts that the construction remains the most compact in parameter efficiency as Markov order and sequence length increase, extending the explicit contribution claim.

C2.justification: A new Section 4 note explains that the construction need not be unique and connects its design to empirical attention patterns and prior theory. Appendix H adds interpretations of sensitivity to corrupted dependencies, greater robustness to transition perturbations than token substitution, and preservation of attention structure at 8-bit precision.

D1.justification: The anonymous code-access link is replaced with a named GitHub repository link. Figure 2 newly states that experiments use standard initialization, and the added experiments document corruption and quantization procedures. Existing hardware, runtime, optimizer, and hyperparameter information is retained in relocated Appendix H.5.

R1.justification: The related-work section and 37-entry bibliography are retained. The introduction and new Appendix I expand parameter-efficiency positioning against Rajaraman et al. and Nichani et al., including revised accounting and an explicit claim about efficiency as sequence length and order grow.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 adds a construction-motivation note and introductory quotation, expands notation explanations, repairs cross-references, updates author and publication text, and extends the appendix organization for the new studies and parameter breakdown.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands evidence displays with Figures 17–20, depth and noise result tables, an unnumbered quantization table, and parameter-breakdown Tables 6–7. Figures 5, 9, and 13 remove uninformative first-layer pseudo-attention and difference panels. The original experimental-settings table is relocated and renumbered as Table 5.

improvement.justification: v2 improves support and auditability through the MLP scaling correction, quantitative depth and robustness evidence beyond v1's attention visualizations, and explicit uncertainty reporting. The central theoretical results remain unchanged. The new accounting also contains an inconsistency: Table 7's component rows imply a linear constant of 12(6S + 3), while its total uses 10(6S + 3). This limits the benefit of the expanded parameter analysis but does not outweigh the overall gains.
